answer:
**Raise prices carefully now; wait on the second van.** Capacity is your constraint, and pricing can improve this year’s earnings immediately.

Using 52 weeks ÷ 12, you complete approximately 156 grooms monthly:

- Revenue: 156 × $95 = **$14,820**.
- Contribution per groom: $95 − $38 wages − $12 = **$45**.
- Monthly cash surplus: 156 × $45 − $3,800 = **$3,220**, before owner pay, taxes and unlisted costs. Loan principal makes this different from accounting profit.

**Days 1–30:** Price new customers at an average $110. Give regulars 30 days’ notice of a move to $100; honor existing quoted appointments. With the same 70/30 mix, the eventual average ticket becomes $103. Contribution becomes $49.80, producing **$3,969 monthly surplus—$749 more**, assuming unchanged volume. Booked appointments will delay that increase.

Prebook regulars’ next two visits at their appropriate 6–8-week intervals before releasing remaining availability. Cluster appointments geographically, use reminders and a clear cancellation policy, and fill gaps from a route-matched waitlist. Avoid discounted annual packages that commit scarce capacity cheaply.

**Days 30–90:** Track completed grooms, regulars returning when due, price-related departures and unique waitlist customers accepting $110. Your 70% regular-booking share is not a retention rate.

A second van adds 36 weekly slots; 15 requests fill only **42%**, even if all convert. At $110, 65 monthly grooms contribute $3,510; subtract financing and only **$1,860 remains before additional insurance, maintenance, training and administration**.

Begin recruiting now, but purchase only after trained staff, confirmed bookings exceeding fully costed break-even by 30%, and three months’ operating reserves are secured. Two months’ hiring leaves little operating time before December 31; pricing is the stronger near-term profit move.
